Both earth lurches and slides are known to occur on steep slopes along stream banks. Seismic shaking can overstress weak cohesive (claying) and mixed soils, resulting in slumps and slides along banks. Structures situated within a horizontal distance of about three or four times the height of the bank should be evaluated by a site-specific study.
Seismically-induced inundation can result from tsunami, seiches, and levee failure. Inundation can also result from earthquake produced landslides which form natural dams that are usually relatively unstable and can cause inundation when they fail.
The potential of damage from tsunami in the San Jose area has been calculated based upon Golden Gate tide gauge records and other records and assuming a 20-foot wave runup. The possibility of damage in the San Jose area from a tsunami appears to be extremely remote. Due to the strike-slip movement of the major active faults in the San Francisco Bay region, the likelihood of a locally generated tsunami is equally remote.
The possibility of water-retention dikes failing along Guadalupe and Alviso sloughs to the north of the project is high during a significant earthquake. The areas subject to the greatest hazard are located below elevation 13.5 feet.
C. HYDROLOGY AND WATER QUALITY
Flood Potential
The city of San Jose is drained primarily by the Guadalupe River and Coyote Creek, with Los Gatos Creek and Silver Creek major tributaries of those streams, respectively. These watercourses have experienced repeated historic flooding and have undergone a certain amount of flood control improvements in response to increased urbanization and consequent flood danger.
